etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English crampe, from Old French crampe (“cramp”), from Frankish *krampa (“cramp”), from Proto-West Germanic *krampu, from Proto-Germanic *krampō (“cramp, clasp”). Distant relative of English crop.

definitions.definition: A painful contraction of a muscle which cannot be controlled; (sometimes) a similar pain even without noticeable contraction.

quote.citation: August 1534, Margaret Roper (or Thomas More in her name), letter to Alice Alington
quote.text: the cramp also that divers nights gripeth him in his legs.

quote.citation: 1692, Roger L’Estrange, “ (please specify the fable number.) (please specify the name of the fable.)”, in Fables, of Æsop and Other Eminent Mythologists: […], London:  […]  R[ichard] Sare, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: A narrow Fortune is undoubtedly a Cramp to a great Mind.

quote.citation: 1781 (date written), William Cowper, “Truth”, in Poems, London:  […]  J[oseph] Johnson, […], published 1782, →OCLC, page 96:
quote.text: How does it grate upon his thankleſs ear, / Crippling his pleaſures with the cramp of fear!

definitions.definition: A clamp for carpentry or masonry.
A piece of wood having a curve corresponding to that of the upper part of the instep, on which the upper leather of a boot is stretched to give it the requisite shape.
(intransitive) (of a muscle) To contract painfully and uncontrollably.
(transitive) To affect with cramps or spasms.

quote.citation: 1936, Heinrich Hauser, Once Your Enemy (translated from the German by Norman Gullick)
quote.text: The collar of the tunic scratched my neck, the steel helmet made my head ache, and the puttees cramped my leg muscles.

definitions.definition: (transitive, figurative) To prohibit movement or expression of.

quote.citation: 1853, Austen Henry Layard, Discoveries in the Ruins of Nineveh and Babylon:
quote.text: But the front of the animal , which was in full , was narrow and cramped , and unequal in dignity to the side

definitions.definition: (transitive) To restrain to a specific physical position, as if with a cramp.

quote.text: when the gout cramps my joints

definitions.definition: To fasten or hold with, or as if with, a cramp iron.
(by extension) To bind together; to unite.

quote.text: The  […]  fabric of universal justice is well cramped and bolted together in all its parts.

quote.citation: 1871, David Masson, The Life of John Milton:
quote.text: […]  the result was those folio volumes of MSS. now in the British Museum, in which inquirers into the history of that period find so much interesting material in such a confused state and in such a dreadfully cramp handwriting.
